title: Directed percolation in higher-order social dilemmas
abstract: Multiplayer social dilemmas on hypergraphs show a variety of emergent phenomena, which has been attributed to group interactions. Here we test whether pairwise dynamics can reproduce them as well. We derive the mesoscopic Langevin equation of a testbed model and find the operator content of absorbing phase transitions: a directed-percolation line, a tricritical point, and a first-order region whose spinodal is the explosive transition. In our analysis, three-player games only set the values of the Landau coefficients. We construct a strictly pairwise model with short-lived memory, in which every event involves at most two entities, that reproduces these coefficients term by term and has exactly the same mean-field fixed points. Simulations confirm that the two dynamics share mean-field critical and tricritical scaling and the size of the critical mass, and that a purely three-player game on a two-dimensional triangular lattice lies in the directed-percolation class. For these games, the explosive transition and the critical mass therefore do not require group interactions, and the critical behavior is that of the pairwise theory.
summary: This paper analyzes social dilemmas on hypergraphs to determine if complex, multi-player interactions are necessary for emergent critical behavior. By deriving a mesoscopic Langevin equation, the authors show that a simplified, strictly pairwise model can reproduce the critical exponents and scaling laws of the full higher-order game. This suggests that the critical physics is governed by pairwise dynamics, regardless of the complexity of the underlying group structure.
main_problem: The paper investigates whether emergent phenomena observed in complex, higher-order social dilemmas (on hypergraphs) can be accurately reproduced by simpler, strictly pairwise interaction dynamics.
main_result: The critical behavior (e.g., directed percolation class, critical exponents) of the higher-order games is shown to be equivalent to that of the pairwise theory, suggesting group interactions are not necessary for determining critical scaling.
method: The authors derive a mesoscopic Langevin equation for the dynamics and compare its operator content and critical exponents derived from both the full hypergraph model and a constructed pairwise model.
model_or_system: The model involves players adopting Cooperation or Defection in social dilemmas, ranging from pairwise (2-player) to three-player (3-player) games played on hypergraphs or lattices. The dynamics are governed by payoff differences leading to an effective Langevin equation.
key_observables: Order parameter (cooperator density $ho$), critical exponents ($\delta_s, 	heta, 2/z$), and the location of phase transition lines (Directed-Percolation line, Tricritical Point).
important_parameters: Sucker payoff ($S$), fraction of 3-games ($\delta$), and the dimensionality of the lattice (e.g., 2D triangular lattice).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes that the higher-order dynamics can be mapped onto an effective pairwise dynamics with short-lived memory, and that lattice correlations are irrelevant at the DP fixed point.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the phase diagram showing the DP, TDP, and first-order regions, and later figures show the collapse of density decay curves and the matching of critical exponents between the two dynamics on a triangular lattice.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the mean-field description for higher-order dilemmas, deriving the Langevin equation. It then constructs a strictly pairwise model that reproduces the necessary coefficients. Finally, it compares the critical scaling and dynamics (including 2D lattice simulations) between the two models to demonstrate equivalence.
why_interesting: The work provides a powerful demonstration of universality in complex systems, showing that the critical behavior of high-order interactions can be captured by lower-order, pairwise descriptions, which is a key concept in statistical physics.
analysis_basis: full PDF text, analyzed in chunks
